newsitem.title: USA: Clinical research down as managed care rises-study.
newsitem.headline: Clinical research down as managed care rises-study.

text.p: When managed health care becomes more prevalent in a community, the pace of clinical research sometimes slows, researchers reported on Friday in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA).

To counteract that reported trend, one leading health adviser suggested that health care premiums be taxed at the rate of 1 percent over four years, with the money going directly to clinical research.

The JAMA articles linking an intensely competitive health care marketplace with a decline in clinical research in selected areas represent the "leading edge" in a potentially damaging development, said Dr. Kenneth Shine, president of the Institute of Medicine, which advises the federal government.
"I believe that the effect of this development is such that it will compromise the capacity to bring innovation to health care at the bedside," Shine said at a news conference.
Shine, who wrote a commentary in the July 16 edition of JAMA, said various cities and some states had expressed interest in the notion of taxing managed care to pay for clinical research.
Cuts in Medicare and Medicaid also contribute to the decline in clinical research, Shine said.
Shine said the managed care industry had expressed concern that all companies should participate equally in the efffort to pay for clinical research.
"The recurring theme is a level playing field," he said. "That goes a long way to making them more comfortable.

The American Association of Health Plans, which represents more than 1,000 managed health care plans in the United States, said the JAMA studies gave an "incomplete and misleading" view of the relationship between managed care companies and clinical research.

Nevertheless, the group's president Karen Ignagni said in a statement, "We would be very pleased to participate in discussions of how health plans can best contribute to establishing priorities for and advancing the nation's clinical research agenda."

Bolstering Shine's push for a different way to raise money for clinical research, Dr. Ernest Moy wrote in JAMA that medical schools in markets with a high level of managed health care appeared less likely to get federal research grants than those where managed care was less pervasive.
Moy declined at the news conference to say that pressures of managed health care caused the decline.
A third article found that in the most competitive health care markets, fewer scientific articles were published, doctors had more patient care duties and perceived more stress.
Authors of this article warned that failure to protect clinical research from the full effect of market competition might mean that basic research findings will take longer to get to patients.
